items.prompt: Try it: move the white knight on g1 to any square you think it can reach. A wrong try costs nothing.

claims.statement: From g1 the knight can go to exactly e2, f3 and h3.
The knight cannot move straight up two squares.
The knight cannot move one square diagonally.

hints: The knight does not move in a straight line, and it does not move one step like a king.
Think of a letter L: two squares in one direction, then one square to the side.
One answer is f3: go two squares up, then one square to the left.
items.explain: A knight on g1 can land on e2, f3 or h3: each is two squares one way and one square to the side. The squares straight ahead or diagonally next to it are not on its list.

feedback_by_move.g1g3: That is two squares straight up. The knight needs one more step to the side after two up, so g3 is not a landing square.
feedback_by_move.g1f2: That is one step diagonally, like a king or bishop. A knight jumps in an L, so f2 is not a landing square.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white knight on e5 can jump to. The board holds only the knight and the two kings, so every L-shaped jump that stays on the board is possible.

claims.statement: The knight on e5 has exactly these eight landing squares.

hints: Work around the knight like a clock: two squares up and one across each way, then two across and one up or down each way.
Two up from e5 is e7. One square to the side of e7 gives d7 and f7.
There are eight landing squares in all, two in each direction: up, down, left and right.
items.explain: The knight on e5 jumps two squares up or down and one to the side (d7, f7, d3, f3), or two squares left or right and one up or down (c6, c4, g6, g4). That makes eight, because the board is open around it.

items.prompt: A white knight stands on a2, one square up from the corner. How many squares can it jump to? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The knight on a2 can go to exactly b4, c1 and c3.

hints: Picture the eight L-shaped jumps and cross out the ones that would leave the board.
From a2, every jump to the left leaves the board, and so does every jump two squares down.
Only b4, c3 and c1 stay on the board.
items.explain: From a2 the jumps to the left and the jumps two squares down would leave the board. That leaves b4, c3 and c1: three. The corner gives two, this square three, and a3 four.

items.prompt: The knight on g1 wants to reach e5 in two jumps. Which first jump makes that possible?

claims.statement: The knight can jump to f3.
After g1 to f3 the knight reaches e5 with its next jump.
After g1 to e2 the knight cannot reach e5 next.
After g1 to h3 the knight cannot reach e5 next.

hints: A knight has three possible first jumps here. Test each one: from there, is e5 an L away?
From the right first square, e5 is two squares up and one to the left.
There are only three first jumps, so test them one at a time: exactly one of them leaves e5 an L away.
items.explain: From f3 the knight is two squares below and one square to the side of e5, so one more jump reaches it. From e2 or h3, e5 is not an L away.

feedback_by_move.g1e2: From e2 the squares an L away are c1, c3, d4, f4, g1 and g3. None is e5.
feedback_by_move.g1h3: From h3 the squares an L away are f2, f4, g1 and g5. None is e5.

items.prompt: Tap every white piece that can move to f5.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 can jump to f5.
The bishop on c8 can slide to f5.
The rook on f2 can slide to f5.
The knight on e5 cannot move one square sideways.
Exactly three white pieces reach f5.

hints: Go through the white pieces one at a time and ask how each one moves.
A bishop needs a clear diagonal, a rook a clear file or rank. For a knight, ask: is f5 one of its eight L-squares?
Two white pieces slide to f5 and one knight jumps there. The other knight is right next to f5, which is not an L away.
items.explain: The knight on d4 jumps to f5 (two across, one up). The bishop on c8 slides down the diagonal through d7 and e6. The rook on f2 slides up the open f-file. The knight on e5 stands next to f5 and one step sideways is not a knight move.

items.prompt: White to move. The knight on c3 can capture exactly one black piece. Capture it.

claims.statement: The knight can capture the bishop on e4.
The knight cannot capture the pawn on d4.
The knight cannot capture the rook on c5.

hints: Look at all eight L-squares around c3 and find the black piece standing on one of them.
The pawn on d4 and the rook on c5 look close, but check whether each is an L away.
The target is two squares to the right and one up.
items.explain: The bishop on e4 is two squares right and one up from c3: an L. The pawn on d4 is one step diagonally and the rook on c5 is two squares straight up, and neither of those is a knight jump.

feedback_by_move.c3d4: The pawn on d4 is one step diagonally from the knight. A knight cannot take that way, so this move is not legal.
feedback_by_move.c3c5: The rook is two squares straight up. A knight always turns a corner, so this move is not legal.

items.prompt: The knight on d4 will jump twice. Can it be standing on d5 after those two jumps? Think about square colours, then answer.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 has exactly eight landing squares.
After d4 to b3 the knight does not attack d5.
After d4 to b5 the knight does not attack d5.
After d4 to c2 the knight does not attack d5.
After d4 to c6 the knight does not attack d5.
After d4 to e2 the knight does not attack d5.
After d4 to e6 the knight does not attack d5.
After d4 to f3 the knight does not attack d5.
After d4 to f5 the knight does not attack d5.

hints: Each jump changes the colour of the square the knight stands on. What colour is d4, and what colour is d5?
d4 is a dark square and d5 is a light one. After one jump the knight is on light, after two it is back on dark.
So two jumps always end on the colour you started on, and d5 is the other colour.
items.explain: d4 is dark and d5 is light. One jump changes the colour and the second changes it back, so after two jumps the knight is on a dark square again. It would need an odd number of jumps to reach d5.

items.prompt: The knight on a1 wants to reach b2, a square of the same colour. What is the smallest number of jumps it needs?

claims.statement: The knight on a1 can go only to b3 and c2.
After a1 to b3 the knight does not attack b2.
After a1 to c2 the knight does not attack b2.
After three jumps (c2, a3, c4) the knight attacks b2, so the fourth jump arrives.

hints: Same colour means an even number of jumps, so it is 2 or 4. Can two jumps do it?
The two first squares from a1 are b3 and c2. Is b2 an L away from either?
Neither is, so two jumps fail. Try the route c2, a3, c4 and then b2.
items.explain: Same colour needs an even number of jumps. From b3 or c2, b2 is not an L away, so two jumps are not enough. The route a1, c2, a3, c4, b2 takes four. Corner squares are awkward for a knight.

items.prompt: Your turn to use what you know. White to move: find the knight jump that attacks two black pieces at once, one of them the king.

claims.statement: The knight can jump to f6.
The jump to f6 wins the queen for at most a knight at the end of best play.

hints: Look for a landing square that is an L away from both the king on g8 and the queen on d7.
Check each of the eight squares around the knight. Which one is two columns from d7 and an L from g8?
The answer is on the f-file, in the black camp.
items.explain: From f6 the knight attacks the king on g8 and the queen on d7. The king must answer the check, and then the knight takes the queen. Nothing can block a knight check.

items.prompt: Tap every square the white knight on c3 can move to. Own pieces count.

claims.statement: The knight on c3 can go to exactly six squares: a4 and e2 hold its own pieces.

hints: List the eight landing squares first, then look at what stands on each.
A landing square holding one of your own pieces is not available. An enemy piece there can be taken.
Two of the eight squares are blocked by white pieces; one of the others holds a black pawn you may capture.
items.explain: Of the eight landing squares, a4 holds a white pawn and e2 a white bishop, so those two are out. The black pawn on d5 can be captured, so d5 counts. That leaves a2, b1, b5, d1, d5 and e4.
